section_summary: This section covers Japan’s efforts to expand exports and become economically self-supporting. Airgrams report on copper sales, shipping, Sterling Area trade and trade procedures; a despatch encloses four speeches on Japan’s economic prospects. The section then introduces a proposed economic rehabilitation plan for 1953, including its assumptions, priorities and production and trade targets.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Airgram A-226 on Economic and Trade Developments
subfiles.from: U.S. Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports on copper sales, Japanese shipping, Sterling Area trade and proposed changes to trade administration.
subfiles.summary: The mission describes inquiries into possible diversion of Japanese copper to Eastern Europe and discusses whether Japan could expand its merchant shipping. It also reports revived Sterling Area negotiations, a freight conference investigation, stalled import and export procedure changes, and proposals concerning Japanese travel abroad.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 631 Forwarding Four Speeches on Japanese Self-Support
subfiles.from: U.S. Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards four speeches on how Japan might become self-supporting.
subfiles.summary: The despatch outlines Fine’s proposals for exports, production, shipping and regional trade, then comments on the other speakers’ views. It highlights agricultural potential, particularly in Hokkaido.

subfiles.title: Sherwood M. Fine Speech: How Can Japan Become a Self-Supporting Nation?
subfiles.to: America’s Town Meeting of the Air audience
subfiles.about: Sets out seven measures to close Japan’s import and export gap.
subfiles.summary: Fine calls for increased exports and domestic production, fewer trade barriers, Japanese shipping, tourism, foreign investment and closer economic exchange with Asian neighbors.

subfiles.title: Akira Kodaki Speech: How Can Japan Become a Self-Supporting Nation?
subfiles.to: America’s Town Meeting of the Air audience
subfiles.about: Argues that skilled labor and fair access to overseas markets could sustain Japan’s economy.
subfiles.summary: Kodaki points to rising exports and seeks wider trade agreements, rebuilt shipping, foreign investment, tourism and nondiscriminatory treatment of Japanese goods.

subfiles.title: Kiichiro Satoh Speech: How Can Japan Become a Self-Supporting Nation?
subfiles.to: America’s Town Meeting of the Air audience
subfiles.about: Discusses population growth, food supply and trade as obstacles to Japanese self-support.
subfiles.summary: Satoh advocates birth control, expanded fishing and shipping, and greater foreign trade to improve employment and living standards.

subfiles.title: Emeny Speech: How Can Japan Become a Self-Supporting Nation?
subfiles.to: America’s Town Meeting of the Air audience
subfiles.about: Connects Japan’s self-support to agricultural improvement and the wider economy of the Far East.
subfiles.summary: The speaker proposes fuller use of farmland, waterpower and transport, review of the purge of Japanese leaders, and a regional policy that recognizes Japan’s economic ties to Asia.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Airgram A-233 on Trade Investigations and Sterling Area Negotiations
subfiles.from: U.S. Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Updates the Department on copper, freight, trade administration and export problems.
subfiles.summary: Officials decide to seek investigation of alleged copper transshipments while continuing export sales. The airgram also covers the freight conference case, visiting U.S. trade advisers, weak Sterling Area purchasing prospects, travel clearance delays, resistance within Japan’s trade ministry and uncertainty over export floor prices.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Airgram A-243 on Narcotics Restitution and Copper Sales
subfiles.from: U.S. Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports a request for restituted narcotics and publicity about suspected copper transshipments.
subfiles.summary: The legible opening reports an alleged attempt to obtain restituted opium and a United Press story on possible copper sales behind the Iron Curtain. Later items concern Japanese trade administration, but the OCR is too damaged for a reliable account of their details.

subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum Regarding Attached Trade Material
subfiles.to: W. Walton Butterworth; Willard L. Thorp
subfiles.about: Routes attached material concerning Japanese trade issues.
subfiles.summary: A routing memorandum with comments largely obscured by poor OCR.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 669 Forwarding Translation of Economic Rehabilitation Plan
subfiles.from: U.S. Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards and assesses a proposed Japanese economic rehabilitation plan.
subfiles.summary: The despatch explains the plan’s preparation, its proposed path to self-support by 1953 and the decision against publishing it as government policy. It questions some trade comparisons and describes the plan’s emphasis on chemicals, ceramics, domestic resources, industrial expansion and reduced dependence on American aid.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 671 Forwarding Survey of Interest in Zaibatsu Stocks
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards a public opinion survey on purchasing zaibatsu securities.
subfiles.summary: The survey found little public understanding or interest, though the stockholder base had widened.

subfiles.title: Economic Rehabilitation Planning Committee Report
subfiles.about: Proposes a five-year program for Japan to reach a self-supporting economy by 1953.
subfiles.summary: The report assesses losses from war and colonial separation, population growth, trade constraints, inflation, subsidies, depleted capital and low productivity. It proposes priorities for stabilization, exports, power, coal, steel, transport, food production and disaster prevention, with particular emphasis on manufacturing and chemicals. Tables project population, production, imports, exports and international payments through 1953. The report continues beyond page 68.
